sections.body:
A bubble is a period when prices detach from the underlying value of what is being sold. A revolution is a period when technology genuinely changes what economies can do. The uncomfortable truth is that they look identical while they are happening: both involve excitement, rapid investment, wild claims and fortunes made early.

History offers both templates. The dot-com bubble destroyed trillions in paper wealth — and left behind the fiber, the habits and the companies that built the modern internet. The railway manias ruined many investors — and left the tracks that transformed continents. Railroads were a bubble and a revolution at the same time.

So the honest question about AI is not "bubble or revolution?" as if one excludes the other. It is: which specific claims are inflated, which capabilities are real, and how much time separates today's prices from today's value? Those are separable questions with separable answers.
examples: The investor who lost everything on a railway stock and the society that gained everything from the railway were both right about different things.
sections.heading: Bubbles and revolutions look identical at first

sections.body:
Analysts describe a recurring pattern called the hype cycle: a technology emerges, expectations soar beyond what it can deliver, disappointment follows, and then — if the technology is real — steady adoption builds on actual value. The internet, mobile computing and blockchain all traced versions of this curve.

AI has lived several small hype cycles already, and the current wave is the largest. Some signals match the top of the cycle: valuations that assume future profits, products rebranded around intelligence they barely use, and revenue promises that count pilots as sales. Other signals match genuine revolution: measurable productivity in programming and translation, scientific discovery accelerated, and a flood of real applications nobody planned.

The position on the curve matters less than the discipline of the observer. Anyone evaluating AI should be able to name, for their own domain, which capabilities are proven, which are promising, and which are vapor — and update the map every few months, because this curve moves fast.
examples: The company saved real money using AI for customer support — and quietly cancelled the 'AI strategy' project that had generated the press releases.
sections.heading: The hype cycle and where AI stands

sections.body:
Economic value has a stubborn test: does someone, somewhere, pay less or earn more because of this technology, in amounts that survive the pilot phase? Under that test, AI's strongest results cluster in specific places: code generation, where output per developer is measurably up; language tasks, where translation and drafting save hours; and pattern recognition in science, where models find structures humans missed.

The weakest claims share a shape: value that exists only on a slide deck. "Transformed workflows" without changed headcount. "Intelligence" that is a search box with new branding. Revenue from selling access to models that lose money on every query, made up in volume.

This is why sober evaluation always returns to unit economics: what does it cost to deliver this capability, what is it worth to the user, and who captures the difference? Inflated expectations are not lies exactly — they are bets placed on a future where the answers will be better. Sometimes the future pays. The skill is knowing which bets you are personally standing under.
examples: The AI feature customers actually pay for is the boring one — the form that fills itself — not the impressive demo.
sections.heading: What real value looks like

sections.body: These terms separate the analysis of AI from the excitement around it.
sections.heading: The vocabulary of hype and value

terms.example: Critics of the AI bubble point to startups valued at billions with revenue in the millions.
terms.gloss: A period in which investment and valuations in AI exceed the technology's near-term economic value.

terms.example: The hype cycle for virtual reality has had two peaks and two troughs so far.
terms.gloss: The observed pattern in which new technologies pass through inflated expectations, disappointment, and eventual steady adoption.

terms.example: The market valuation assumed growth that would require every company on earth to buy the product.
terms.gloss: The total price investors place on a company or sector, reflecting expected future profits rather than current ones.

terms.example: The productivity paradox of computers lasted decades before the gains finally appeared in the statistics.
terms.gloss: The historical lag between the arrival of a transformative technology and its measurable effect on economic productivity.

terms.example: Due diligence revealed that the 'AI platform' was three contractors with a chat interface.
terms.gloss: The investigation of claims, numbers and risks before committing money or reputation.

terms.example: The unit economics of the service were upside down: each query cost more to run than the customer paid.
terms.gloss: The revenue and cost attached to one unit of a product — the arithmetic of whether a business model works.

sections.body: Even if the bubble thesis is right, the conclusion is rarely that the technology is fake. The conclusion is that prices were wrong and weak companies die while the capability survives and matures. Bubbles destroy investors; they rarely destroy technologies.
sections.heading: Bubbles pop; revolutions continue

sections.body:
For anyone deciding where to stand — as an investor, an employee, a builder or a citizen — a few questions cut through most of the noise. **What is proven in production here, not in demos?** **Whose money is being spent, and is it earned or invested?** **If the valuation fell by half tomorrow, would the underlying work still matter?** **What would make this claim false, and is anyone checking?**

The same discipline applies to doom as to hype. Claims that AI will imminently replace all knowledge work deserve the same scrutiny as claims that it will solve everything — both are bets on extrapolation, and extrapolation is where errors breed.

The likeliest outcome, if history is a guide, is the untidy one: a genuine revolution with a spectacular financial accident somewhere inside it. The internet survived the crash; the crash was terrible. Holding both facts at once — the real capability and the real risk — is the adult position in a loud market.
examples: She joined the AI team because the problems were real and the customers were paying — and keeps her savings far from the stock.
sections.heading: A sober framework for a loud market

item.summary: Trillions are invested, valuations soar, and every product announces intelligence. Is this the internet of 1995 or the tulips of 1637? This article examines how to think about AI hype: the difference between a bubble and a revolution, what real economic value looks like, and how inflated expectations can coexist with genuine technology.
item.title: AI Bubble or Real Revolution?
